newsitem.title: MEXICO: OLYMPIC CITIES TO AVOID "JUNK" COMMERCIALISM IN FUTURE.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPIC CITIES TO AVOID "JUNK" COMMERCIALISM IN FUTURE.

text.p: Cities hosting the Olympic Games in the future will be bound by contract to avoid excessive "junk" commercialism of the kind which many felt marred the 1996 Atlanta Games, Olympic officials said Thursday.

"The problem in Atlanta was the street vending programme, which was junk," International Olympic Committee (IOC) vice president Dick Pound told reporters during a four-day IOC board meeting here. "This was a big disappointment to us."

Although nothing can be written into host city contracts until 2004 -- the Summer and Winter Games have already been assigned for the years until then -- Pound said future contracts would specifically bar host city authorities from excessive or degrading commercialism.

In the meantime, the goodwill or common sense of the host cities -- Nagano in Japan and Salt Lake City in the United States for the 1998 and 2002 Winter Games, and Sydney for the 2000 Summer Games -- should rein in commercial excess, he said.
"Fortunately the next three host cities were there...they saw what the city of Atlanta did to itself and its Games and went away understanding that they must never do that themselves," Pound said.

"For our part the next time we do a host city contract you can be sure that the Atlanta experience will be reflected in the new contract and that the host city as a signatory to the contract will have to agree specifically not to do anything like this."
In the case of Atlanta, Pound said the blame appeared to lie with the city authorities themselves rather than with the Games organising committee or U.S. Olympic authorities.

Atlanta organising committee president Bill Payne earlier told the IOC board that the $1.7 billion Games, funded entirely by the private sector, would break even and even show a small surplus, probably of somewhere below $10 million.
Atlanta would receive a legacy worth some $500 million in paid-for sports facilities, he added, shrugging off charges of excess commercialism.
"Only in America does the private sector support the Games to this overwhelming extent," he said.
Both Payne and Pound said there was no discussion of the commercialism question nor of other glitches at the Games such as transportation and communications difficulties.
Pound said that initial television audience data showed that in brute terms the worldwide Atlanta viewership jumped sharply compared to the 1992 Barcelona Games.
"The cumulative audience is up 15 percent to 20 percent over Barcelona, we think (there were) between 19 and 20 billion viewers," he said.

Earlier, IOC president Joan Antonio Samaranch stressed the need for continued government involvement in Olympic events. IOC officials have expressed concern at the lack of a safety net of state funding for the Atlanta Games and at the lack of coordination with city authorities.

In an opening address to the Association of National Olympic Committees, which is also meeting in Cancun, Samaranch said he was glad to see that an Australian government official was heading the organisation committee for the 2000 Sydney Olympics.

The presence of Michael Knight, New South Wales Olympics minister, at the helm would be "a useful bridge, a necessary bridge, so that relations between the government and the organising committee are as fluid as possible."
"This has been a lesson of the past which we must learn from in the present and in the future," Samaranch said.
Officials said Thursday that the IOC had approved a 1997 budget of 37 million Swiss francs, up almost 15 percent from 1996.
